hints: Because the array is sorted, avoid checking every element from left to right.
Think of the answer as the first index whose value is greater than or equal to target.
If nums[mid] is too small, the answer must be to the right; otherwise, the answer is at mid or to the left.
When the search finishes, the left boundary is the insertion position.
title: Search Insert Position Problem

notes: The returned index is the first position whose value is greater than or equal to target.
If target is greater than every element, return nums.length.
constraints: nums contains distinct integers sorted in ascending order.
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array containing the two arguments [nums, target].
content.outputFormat: Single line: JSON-serialised integer representing the index at which target is found or should be inserted.

sampleTestCases.explanation: Target 5 is already present at index 2.
Target 2 is not present; inserting it between 1 and 3 keeps the array sorted, so the index is 1.
Target 7 is greater than every element, so it would be inserted after index 3, at index 4.

content.problemStatement:
You receive a sorted array of distinct integers and a target value, output the index if the target is found. If not, output the index where it would be if it were inserted in order.

You must write an algorithm with `O(log n)` runtime complexity.

notes: Solutions are expected to satisfy the required O(log n) runtime complexity.
This is a lower-bound binary search.
The same algorithm handles an exact match, insertion at the beginning, insertion in the middle, and insertion at the end.
solution.approach: Use binary search to find the lower bound of target: the first index i such that nums[i] >= target. Maintain a search interval [left, right]. When nums[mid] is at least target, move right to mid - 1; otherwise move left to mid + 1. When the loop ends, left is exactly the required insertion position.

better.complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) extra space.
better.description: Because the array is sorted, binary search removes the need for linear scanning. There is no necessary intermediate asymptotic approach between the linear scan and the optimal lower-bound binary search for this contract.

optimal.complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) extra space.
optimal.description: Perform lower-bound binary search. If nums[mid] >= target, the answer is at mid or to its left, so set right = mid - 1. Otherwise target must be to the right, so set left = mid + 1. When the search interval becomes empty, left is the first valid insertion position. This also returns nums.length when target is larger than every element.

bruteForce.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
bruteForce.description: Scan the array from left to right and return the first index whose value is greater than or equal to target. If no such index exists, return nums.length.

followUps: How would the solution change if duplicate values were allowed and the first occurrence were required?
How would you implement the same lower-bound operation using a language's standard library?
What changes would be needed if the array were sorted in descending order?
